title: Periodically modulated traveling waves in integrate-and-fire networks: recursive speed law and propagation failure
authors: Jie Nissel, Ricardo Erazo-Toscano, Rosahn Bhattarai, Marius Osan, Mandeep Chauhan, Remus Osan
abstract: Traveling waves of activity in neural tissue can be halted by spatial inhomogeneity in synaptic coupling. We study an integrate-and-fire network in which each neuron fires once and the coupling decays exponentially. For this model the leading-edge firing map reduces exactly to a scalar equation for the wave speed in space, with a slow unstable and a fast stable homogeneous speed, $c_1$ and $c_2$, and a periodic modulation of the coupling enters this equation pointwise. Positive periodic waves terminate in folds. For slowly varying modulation the fold amplitude approaches a plateau set by the trough of the modulation, where the local bottleneck speed is $\sqrt{c_1 c_2}$; the approach to the plateau is set by the local geometry of the trough. For rapidly varying modulation the fold amplitude grows linearly with frequency, with a slope given by a full-amplitude average over the integrated modulation profile; a weak-ripple truncation of that average overestimates the slope about 2.5-fold at the default coupling. A perturbative recursion in the amplitude gives the speed profile explicitly. We distinguish loss of the periodic wave from failure of a particular launch, and the excitatory regime $ε\le 1$ from its sign-changing extension. The results are checked against direct integration of the reduced equation and first-spike firing-map simulations of the network.
summary: This work analyzes traveling waves in spiking neural networks subjected to periodic spatial coupling variations. It derives a reduced speed law and determines that wave propagation failure is dictated by the modulation's local minimum (trough) in the slow limit, or by a linear frequency dependence in the fast limit. The findings provide quantitative criteria for understanding how disorder limits activity propagation in biological models.
main_problem: The paper investigates how periodic spatial inhomogeneities in synaptic coupling affect traveling waves of activity in integrate-and-fire neural networks, focusing on the resulting speed law and conditions for wave propagation failure.
main_result: The failure mechanism depends on the modulation's variation: for slow changes, failure is governed by the trough of the modulation, while for rapid changes, the failure amplitude grows linearly with frequency. The speed law is characterized by two distinct homogeneous speeds, $c_1$ and $c_2$.
method: The analysis involves reducing the leading-edge firing map to a scalar ODE, employing perturbative recursion, and analyzing the system in different modulation regimes (slowly vs. rapidly varying).
model_or_system: The system is an integrate-and-fire neural network where synaptic coupling decays exponentially and is subjected to a periodic modulation $K(y)$. The dynamics are governed by an acceleration-speed relation derived from the firing map.
key_observables: Wave speed profile $c(x)$, fold amplitude (failure criterion), and launch threshold (failure criterion).
important_parameters: Modulation frequency ($\omega$), coupling strength ($\epsilon$), and the ratio of time constants ($	au_1, 	au_2$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the exponential decay of coupling allowing reduction to a scalar law, and the $\epsilon > 1$ regime is treated as a hypothesized extension.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the periodic speed profile under alternating modulation, compare analytical solutions to direct simulations, and present phase diagrams defining the launch threshold $\epsilon_f$ for various modulation shapes.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the reduced ODE for the leading edge, then analyzes the behavior under slow and fast modulation limits, providing explicit solutions for piecewise-constant and cosine modulations, and finally discusses the distinction between wave loss and launch failure.
why_interesting: The study of wave propagation failure in complex, non-linear systems like neural networks provides an analogy for understanding pattern formation and stability in many-body systems, which can relate to phase transitions or localization phenomena in condensed matter.

FIG. 4: Speed-band endpoints (c0, cf) traced as ϵ increases, at fixed λ = 1 (Eqs. 14–15). The blue curve is the locus of the minimum (c0) and maximum (cf) wave speeds as ϵ grows from 0 to ϵf. At ϵ = 0 both equal the homogeneous speed c2 (black square, on the c0 = cf diagonal); as ϵ grows the band widens (c0 falls, cf rises) until propagation fails at ϵf ≈1.29, where the stable periodic wave meets an unstable periodic orbit in a fold ((c0, cf) ≈(0.08, 6.2), red). Inset: ϵ along the branch near the fold; the stable wave (solid) and the unstable orbit (dashed) meet at ϵf, where c0 is still above the threshold cp1 ≈0.05 (dotted).

FIG. 5: Convergence of the speed series. Maximum error En = maxx |c(n) −c| over one period of the order-n truncation versus the numerically integrated speed (ω = π, default parameters), for several amplitudes ϵ. The error decreases geometrically with order, rapidly for small ϵ (reaching ∼10−11 by sixth order at ϵ = 0.1) and progressively more slowly as ϵ approaches 1; six orders do not determine the radius of convergence (see text). The dotted line is the numerical floor δnum ≈rtolc2 set by the reference-integration tolerance; errors at or below it reflect integration/interpolation noise rather than truncation.
